title: Raindrops are tiny lightning bolts, and they’re corroding cars, study finds
gist: A Max Planck Institute study found that raindrops sliding across insulating surfaces accumulate electrostatic charge (up to 9,000 volts) that, on impact, generates an electric field strong enough to punch a miniature dielectric-breakdown hole through even chemically resistant coatings like Teflon, exposing the underlying metal to conventional corrosion — a previously unrecognized mechanism relevant to coatings for bridges, hulls, aircraft, and outdoor electronics.

themes.theme: New corrosion mechanism: electrical breakdown, not just abrasion

insights.claim: Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research (led by Zhongyuan Ni, Rüdiger Berger, and Hans-Jürgen Butt) found that charged water drops can electrically punch a hole through an insulating surface coating on impact, rather than corrosion occurring only through the traditional mechanism of chemical dissolution and abrasion.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
entities: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research
insights.so_what: This overturns the design assumption behind most anti-corrosion coatings (paints, polymer films, oxide layers), which are engineered to resist chemical/abrasive attack, not electrical breakdown — implying an entire class of protective coatings used across industries may be under-engineered for a real-world failure mode.
insights.quote: Not scratch it. Not slowly dissolve it. Electrically blow a hole in it, the way a spark jumps a gap.
insights.locator: A new study led by Zhongyuan Ni

insights.claim: Water drops sliding across an insulating surface (leaf, painted wall, windowpane, plastic panel) undergo 'slide electrification,' stripping charge from the surface and building up voltages that have been measured at up to 9,000 volts.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
entities: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research
insights.so_what: 9,000-volt charge accumulation from ordinary rain sliding on common surfaces is a striking, previously under-quantified physical effect with wide potential relevance across coated infrastructure and electronics.
insights.quote: Drops charged this way have been measured at up to 9,000 volts.
insights.locator: The starting point of the study

insights.claim: In lab tests, 35-microliter salted water drops slid down a 50-degree tilted surface, picked up charge, then fell onto a copper plate coated with a 60-nanometer Teflon film; after 3,000 drops (about one afternoon of moderate rain) the Teflon-coated copper had corroded, while drops that fell without sliding (uncharged) left the surface pristine after the same number of impacts.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
entities: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research
insights.so_what: The controlled comparison (charged vs. uncharged drops) is strong causal evidence isolating electrical charge, not just moisture or impact force, as the corrosion driver — a clean experimental result likely to hold up to scrutiny and drive follow-on coatings research.
insights.quote: After 3,000 drops, roughly equivalent to an afternoon of moderate rain, the copper plate beneath all four surfaces had corroded, despite its Teflon coating.

insights.claim: High-speed camera footage showed charged drops deforming into a 'Taylor cone' shape as they approached the copper plate, evidence that the electric field between drop and metal grew strong enough to overcome water's surface tension before contact — and modeling showed a two-nanocoulomb drop reaches 60 kilovolts per millimeter (Teflon's breakdown threshold) while still about 10 micrometers from the surface.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
entities: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research
insights.so_what: This is the mechanistic 'smoking gun' — direct visual and quantitative evidence of dielectric breakdown occurring at the moment of drop impact, giving materials scientists a specific physical threshold (kilovolts per millimeter) to design coatings against.
insights.quote: A drop carrying two nanocoulombs, they found, reaches 60 kilovolts per millimeter, the breakdown threshold of Teflon—the electric field strength at which an insulator stops insulating.
insights.locator: The field’s strength should keep climbing

insights.claim: Charge transfer on impact is nearly total: a drop arriving with two nanocoulombs deposited 1.8 nanocoulombs into the copper and bounced away with only 0.016 nanocoulombs, less than 1 percent of its starting charge.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
entities: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research
insights.so_what: Near-complete charge transfer per drop, repeated over millions of raindrops in real weather, implies the breakdown effect is not a rare edge case but a routine, cumulative process across any charged-rain exposure.
insights.quote: a drop arriving with two nanocoulombs dumped 1.8 of them into the copper on impact and bounced away with 0.016 nanocoulombs, less than 1 percent of what it started with

themes.theme: Coating thickness and scope of exposure

insights.claim: Coating thickness determines vulnerability to this electrical breakdown effect: 12-micrometer polystyrene films were punched through by charged drops while 130-micrometer films survived, because spreading the same voltage across a greater distance drops the field strength below the material's breakdown tolerance.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
entities: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research
insights.so_what: Thicker coatings are a straightforward mitigation, but the article notes this isn't always feasible (optical films must stay clear, aircraft coatings must stay light, electronics housings are thin by design) — a concrete engineering trade-off for coatings suppliers and end-industries to address.
insights.quote: The 130-micrometer polystyrene films came through untouched because spreading the same voltage across ten times the distance drops the field below what the material can tolerate.

insights.claim: The researchers argue this electrical-breakdown corrosion mechanism has broad real-world relevance to any composite material where a conductive or high-permittivity component sits beneath an insulating coating, including bridges, ship hulls, painted steel, outdoor electronics housings, and metalwork on historic buildings, since charged drops form naturally in clouds, thunderstorms, ocean waves, fountains, waterfalls, and industrial processes like electrostatic spraying and inkjet printing.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
entities: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research
insights.so_what: This broadens the addressable problem well beyond a lab curiosity into infrastructure, transportation, marine, and electronics coatings markets — a potential driver of new coatings R&D, testing standards, and product specifications across those industries.
insights.quote: Anywhere a conductive or high-permittivity component is embedded in an insulating matrix, sliding charged drops should find it. Bridges, hulls, painted steel, the polymer housings of outdoor electronics, and metalwork on historic buildings are all candidates.

insights.claim: Most industrially used paint coatings are only a few micrometers thick, and the researchers note that nanocoulomb-scale charges from ordinary charged rain can break through most of these coatings.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
entities: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research
insights.so_what: If most commercial paint coatings are already within the vulnerable thickness range, this implies a widespread, previously unaccounted-for corrosion pathway across existing painted infrastructure and vehicles, not just a lab-scale finding.
insights.quote: Most of the paint coatings we use are just a few micrometers thick, and the researchers note that nanocoulomb-scale charges can break through most of these.

insights.claim: The researchers conclude that current coating selection is largely based on chemical resistance, and argue what is actually needed is a coating specified for how much electric field it can tolerate.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
entities: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research
insights.so_what: This points to a specific, actionable R&D and product-spec gap for coatings/materials companies: dielectric-breakdown-rated protective coatings could become a new product category or certification standard.
insights.quote: What’s really needed is a coating specified for how much electric field it can tolerate, and most of what we have is picked based on what it resists chemically.
